chunks: "Sure. I'll draw them left to right, inputs on the left, output on the right. A NOT gate, an inverter, is a triangle pointing right with a small circle on the tip.
The triangle is a buffer, which just repeats the input, and the circle is the inversion.
An AND gate is a D shape: flat back where the inputs enter, rounded front, output on the curve, and the output is high only if both inputs are high.
An OR gate has a concave curved back and a pointed, curved front, like a shield, and its output is high if either input is high. Then everything else is those plus a bubble.
Put a bubble on the output of the AND shape and you get NAND. Put it on the output of the OR and you get NOR.
XOR is the OR shape with one extra curved line behind the back, and its output is high when exactly one input is high, so when the inputs differ. XNOR is XOR with a bubble.
I'd label each with its expression: Y equals A-bar, A AND B, A plus B, and so on.
There's also the rectangular IEC style, with an ampersand in the box for AND and greater-or-equal-to-one for OR, but the distinctive shapes are what most US schematics use.
And I should say that a symbol only describes the logic function. Whether it's built from CMOS transistors, relays or a lookup table is a separate question."
